scenario: AITA for ignoring my senior associate’s text | Just to give a background story, I’m a first year associate at a local firm and the senior associate in this story has been with the firm for 3 years. So a few weeks ago, I was feeling a little bit under the weather and threw up as soon as I woke up. I notified my senior associate and told her that I won’t be coming to work as I’m not feeling well. She was a bit disappointed but had no choice but to allow me a sick leave. I sent a few emails to our client as per requested by her the previous day and tried to get some sleep. As I’m trying to get some sleep, she kept on texting me with things that I needed to do. I tried to ignore it and turned off my phone’s notification so I can get some sleep. Around an hour later, she called me and told me that I have to sent her a file (regarding client’s data which she doesn’t have on her laptop) immediately as it is an urgent matter. I sent her the files she wanted and asked her if she’ll need anything else as I’m going to the doctor and won’t be bringing my laptop with me. She said that’s all for now. I went to the doctor, and the doctor said I’m overworked (I’ve been working overtime till 2-3AM for the past 2 months) and needs some rest. On my way home, my senior again texted me and told me to get our client’s billing information (something that she could do herself as she also have their contacts). I did as I’m told as fowarded her with the information. I got home, took the prescribed medicine and fell asleep. I was shocked when I woke up to find my phone with 2 miscalled and 30 new messages from her giving me work to do from home. I felt it was a little bit unfair of her to give me work while I’m on a sick leave and so I ignored the message and didn’t reply her. So, AITA for not replying her text? Notes: English is not my first language, I’m sorry if there’s a lot of grammatical errors.

prediction.raw: This is a nuanced situation, and whether your response was "right" or "wrong" depends on several factors—**professionalism, boundaries, health, and workplace culture**. Based on the details you shared, here’s my analysis: ### **Key Issues in the Scenario:** 1. **Unreasonable Expectations While Sick** – Your senior associate repeatedly texted/called you with work while you were recovering, which is **unprofessional** and **unhealthy**. Sending a sick colleague urgent tasks (especially when she had access to the data herself) is a red flag for poor leadership. 2. **No Clear Policy on Sick Leave** – If the firm expects associates to be "on call" even when ill, that’s a systemic problem. A good workplace respects boundaries when someone is sick. 3. **Your Health Was Prioritized by a Doctor** – The doctor explicitly stated you were overworked and needed rest. **Ignoring her messages was not justifiable—it was necessary** to protect your well-being. 4. **Power Imbalance** – As a first-year associate, you’re in a vulnerable position. Pushing back (even passively) against unreasonable demands is **not wrong**—it’s self-preservation. ### **Was Ignoring Her Messages "Right"?** **Yes, in this case, it was justified.** Here’s why: - **You were sick and recovering** – Your doctor confirmed you needed rest. Work demands should not override health. - **The requests were unreasonable** – She could have done some tasks herself (e.g., billing info), yet she kept sending you work. - **No urgency was justified** – If it was truly urgent, she should have escalated to a manager or supervisor, not keep pestering you. - **Passive resistance is sometimes necessary** – If you had replied, it could have set a precedent for future exploitation. Ignoring her (while documenting the behavior) was a **boundary-setting move**. ### **What You Could Have Done Better:** 1. **Set a Clear Boundary Early** – When you first told her you were sick, you could have said: *"I’m not feeling well and need to rest. I’ll check my emails in the morning, but I won’t be available for urgent tasks right now."* This would have given her a chance to adjust expectations. 2. **Document the Behavior** – If this happens again, keep records (screenshots of messages) in case you need to escalate to HR or a supervisor. 3. **Address It Professionally Later** – If this was a one-time thing, it might be fine. But if it’s a pattern, you should: - **Pull her aside privately** (if comfortable) and say: *"I noticed I was getting work requests while I was sick. I wanted to let you know I need to focus on recovery, and I’d appreciate it if we could discuss priorities when I’m back."* - **Escalate if needed** – If she continues, HR should be involved. ### **Final Verdict: 1 (Not Wrong, but Could Be Improved)** - **Not wrong** because you prioritized your health and set a boundary. - **Could be improved** by being more proactive in communicating your limits upfront. Would you like help drafting a response to her (if you decide to engage) or strategies for handling similar situations in the future? You’re not obligated to work while sick—**your well-being comes first**.
